title: Tilt and revenge
teaches: Tilt is emotion taking over your trade decisions after losses, mistakes or bad breaks; revenge trading is sizing up and trading more to win it back fast; you stop both with rules set before the session: a daily loss limit, a cap on trades, a pause when the urge hits, and smaller size after losses.

facts.quote: Market-wide circuit breakers provide for cross-market trading halts during a severe market decline as measured by a single-day decrease in the S&P 500 Index.
facts.claim: The stock market's own circuit breakers halt trading after a big one-day drop in the S&P 500.

facts.quote: A cross-market trading halt can be triggered at three circuit breaker thresholds—7% (Level 1), 13% (Level 2), and 20% (Level 3).
facts.claim: The market-wide triggers are one-day S&P 500 drops of 7%, 13% and 20%.

facts.quote: A market decline that triggers a Level 1 or Level 2 circuit breaker before 3:25 p.m. will halt market-wide trading for 15 minutes
facts.claim: A Level 1 or Level 2 drop before 3:25 p.m. halts all trading for 15 minutes.

facts.quote: It can be especially difficult to check your emotions at the door when making investment decisions in this kind of environment, which may lead to some costly financial mistakes.
facts.claim: In fast trading it is hard to keep emotions out of decisions, and that can lead to costly mistakes.

facts.quote: Never feel pressured to invest right away.
facts.claim: Feeling you must buy right now is a warning sign, not a reason.

facts.quote: The disposition effect is the tendency of an investor to hold on to losing investments too long and sell winning investments too soon.
facts.claim: The disposition effect is holding losers too long and selling winners too soon.

facts.quote: Individual traders usually overtrade after suffering a significant loss or a series of smaller losses in a long losing streak.
facts.claim: Overtrading usually follows a big loss or a run of smaller ones.

facts.quote: To recoup their capital, or to seek “revenge” on the market after a string of losing trades, they may try to make up profits wherever they can, usually by increasing the size and frequency of their trades.
facts.claim: Revenge trading usually means raising both the size and the number of trades to win losses back.

facts.quote: Take a break: Overtrading may be caused by investors feeling as though they have to make a trade. This often leads to suboptimal trades that end in a loss.
facts.claim: Feeling you have to trade leads to poor trades that often lose; a break is one fix.

facts.quote: will have rules about how much risk they can take (including how many trades are appropriate for them to make). Once they have reached this limit, to continue trading is to do so unsoundly.
facts.claim: Traders set limits on risk and on the number of trades; trading past the limit is unsound.

facts.quote: Craving action, traders often develop a “shotgun blast” approach, buying anything and everything they think might be good. A telltale sign is multiple small positions open concurrently, none of which the trader has a specific plan for.
facts.claim: A burst of positions with no plan behind any of them is a telltale sign of overtrading.

facts.quote: The emotional gap refers to decision-making based on extreme emotions or emotional strains, such as anxiety, anger, fear, or excitement. Emotions are often a key reason why people make irrational choices.
facts.claim: Strong emotions such as anger are a key reason people make irrational choices.

facts.quote: Losing streaks can happen to the best of us, but sometimes a bout of bad luck can actually reflect a problem with our trading strategy.
facts.claim: Losing streaks happen to good traders; sometimes a streak also points to a flaw worth checking.

facts.quote: As a trader works to figure out what needs fixing, there's no harm in reducing the size of your trades. Once your results get back on track, you can increase your risk-taking.
facts.claim: After a string of losses, trade smaller while you review, and size back up once results recover.

facts.quote: If a trader has trouble distancing their emotions from their trading decisions, it's never a bad idea to slow down or even take a break. Cooler heads usually prevail, and trading is no exception.
facts.claim: When emotions are steering your trades, slow down or take a break.

facts.quote: Even a modest losing streak can mess with a trader's head, interfering with their execution and ultimately their profit-loss statement.
facts.claim: Even a small losing streak can hurt your execution and your P&L.

facts.quote: which helps explain the downward spiral of “revenge trading” that fuels many catastrophic trading blowups.
facts.claim: Schwab ties revenge trading to many account blowups.

facts.quote: The first thing to do is step away from the market. This can be hard. Many traders feel a strong urge to jump right back in and start to regain their footing.
facts.claim: After a big loss, step away first, even though the urge to jump back in is strong.

facts.quote: Reduce position size. Less money at risk equals less pressure and clearer thinking. Traders can then increase position size as they demonstrate a new track record of executing their system.
facts.claim: Come back smaller, and add size back as you show you are executing your system again.

facts.quote: Many professional trading systems set stops automatically for losses and profits to eliminate second-guessing in the heat of the moment.
facts.claim: Pros automate exits so they don't have to decide in the emotional moment.

facts.quote: They can also implement “circuit breakers” to prevent additional trading after a certain level of loss in a day.
facts.claim: A trading circuit breaker stops more trading once the day's loss reaches a set level.

facts.quote: Traders should at least have written “if, then” plans to help limit emotion-based actions and prevent additional big losses and should consciously commit to these plans before every trading session.
facts.claim: Write if-then plans and commit to them before each session.

facts.quote: For example, they could pledge to step away for the day if they lose a certain amount of money or take 15 minutes if they feel an urge to break a trading rule.
facts.claim: Example rules: done for the day at a set loss, and a 15-minute break when you feel the urge to break a rule.

facts.quote: The practice may help traders recognize and acknowledge market triggers as they occur and then take steps to avoid or counteract the emotion-based behaviors that typically follow.
facts.claim: Recognising a trigger as it happens is what lets you head off the emotional trade that follows.

facts.quote: The lingering effects of a blowup can hurt a trader's decision-making by slowing down thinking and hindering deeper thought.
facts.claim: The effects of a big loss linger and can keep hurting your decisions afterward.

facts.quote: Revenge trading: Instead of reflecting on the loss and building a strong investment plan, the investor is motivated to take action for a quick gain.
facts.claim: Revenge trading is acting for a quick gain instead of reflecting on the loss.

facts.quote: This can easily backfire, especially if the investor selects stocks they have not carefully considered in terms of their investment knowledge, time horizon and risk tolerance. In some cases, the second loss can be even larger than the first.
facts.claim: Revenge picks are often stocks you haven't studied, and the second loss can be bigger than the first.

facts.quote: I’m not just going to sit here and accept these losses, the investor says. I’m going to make it all back, and then some.
facts.claim: The revenge mindset: refuse to accept the loss and try to make it all back.

facts.quote: Tilt is essentially a more fun way of saying you have a problem with anger in performance.
facts.claim: Tendler: tilt is a problem with anger while you perform.

facts.quote: Anger blinds you from reason, and you feel justified in taking overly aggressive lines vs. an opponent who is constantly re-raising you, or jumping back into a position after getting stopped out for the second time.
facts.claim: Tendler: anger makes overly aggressive moves, like jumping back in after a second stop-out, feel justified.

facts.quote: I identified seven different types of tilt: Run Bad Tilt Hate-losing Tilt Injustice Tilt Mistake Tilt Revenge Tilt Entitlement Tilt Desperation Tilt
facts.claim: Tendler's poker book named seven kinds of tilt, including injustice tilt and revenge tilt.

facts.quote: In The Mental Game of Trading I took the first and last out of that list to narrow it down to five.
facts.claim: His trading book keeps five: hate-losing, injustice, mistake, revenge and entitlement tilt.

facts.quote: For you, Tilt can show up in the opposite way, a very subtle seething, where irritation or frustration can cause you to shut down – you become distracted, quiet, disinterested, or bored.
facts.claim: Tilt can be quiet: irritation that shows up as distraction, silence or boredom.

facts.quote: the anger you feel when in a drawdown or downswing is a consequence of a large amount of Tilt-inducing triggers happening in such a short amount of time that your mind can’t recover.
facts.claim: Many small triggers packed into a short time can add up to tilt.

facts.quote: So Tilt carries over day-over-day, making it easier and easier for you to Tilt.
facts.claim: Tilt can carry over from one day to the next.

facts.quote: He coaches professional athletes, world champion poker players and financial traders.
facts.claim: Tendler coaches athletes, poker players and traders.

facts.quote: This isn’t the worst problem to have if they put firm risk management controls in place about the number of trades/day, or a daily loss-limit, and the market provides plenty of opportunities.
facts.claim: Tendler: firm controls on trades per day, or a daily loss limit, keep the damage in check.

facts.quote: a problem that’s rarely just about losing, but about how your severe reaction to losing ends up costing you more.
facts.claim: The damage comes from your reaction to losing, more than from the loss itself.

facts.quote: Yes, money is the scoreboard in trading, but it is not reliable for measuring performance in the short-term.
facts.claim: Short-term P&L is not a reliable measure of how well you are trading.

facts.quote: when the emotional system becomes overactive, it shuts down higher brain functions, limiting your ability to process information, make correct decisions, translate your thoughts into action, access things you’ve learned recently, and even control your emotions.
facts.claim: Tendler: when emotion runs too high, it limits your ability to make correct decisions.

facts.quote: You’re aware that what you’re doing is wrong, but you can’t stop yourself; it’s like you’re compelled to take excessive risks.
facts.claim: On tilt you can know a trade is wrong and still feel compelled to take it.

facts.quote: You must catch the rise of emotion early, when you still have the mental strength to control them.
facts.claim: Catch the emotion early, while you can still control it.

facts.quote: Catching it early is critical. When emotions get too intense, the mind isn’t powerful enough to stop them and mistakes become inevitable. Seeing it afterwards, is like seeing a trade you missed.
facts.claim: Once emotion gets too intense you can't stop it, so it has to be caught early.

facts.quote: Step 1: Recognizing that your problems have been triggered Step 2: Disrupting the momentum of those emotions Step 3: Injecting Logic Step 4: Using a Strategic Reminder
facts.claim: Tendler's real-time strategy: recognise the trigger, disrupt the momentum, inject logic, use a reminder.

facts.quote: Once you scale up without impairing execution, consolidate that expansion of skill before increasing size again.
facts.claim: Raise size only while execution holds, and settle in before the next step up.

facts.quote: This paper documents strong evidence for behavioral biases among Chicago Board of Trade proprietary traders
facts.claim: The study looked at professional traders at the Chicago Board of Trade.

facts.quote: Our traders appear highly loss-averse, regularly assuming above-average afternoon risk to recover from morning losses.
facts.claim: Those pros regularly took above-average risk in the afternoon to win back morning losses.

facts.quote: losing traders actively purchase contracts at higher prices and sell contracts at lower prices than those that prevailed previously.
facts.claim: Traders chasing a morning loss bought at higher prices and sold at lower prices than just before.

facts.quote: Prices set by loss-averse traders are reversed significantly more quickly than those set by unbiased traders.
facts.claim: Prices set by loss-chasing traders reversed faster than prices set by others.

facts.quote: “break-even effects” (in the presence of prior losses, outcomes which offer a chance to break even are especially attractive)
facts.claim: Break-even effect: after losses, a chance to get back to even looks especially attractive.

facts.quote: a “house money effect” (increased risk seeking in the presence of a prior gain)
facts.claim: House money effect: more risk taking after a gain.

facts.quote: Instead, institutions aggressively reduce risk following losses and mildly increase risk following gains. This asymmetry is more pronounced later in the calendar year and among older and more experienced funds.
facts.claim: In their currency trades, large institutions cut risk hard after losses and added only a little after gains, more so in older, more experienced funds.

facts.quote: Detrimental out-of-control poker decision-making due to negative emotions is known as tilting.
facts.claim: Researchers define tilt as out-of-control decisions driven by negative emotions.

facts.quote: Tilting, in the narratives, was often instigated by dissociative feelings ('unreality', disbelief) following a significant monetary loss.
facts.claim: Tilt often started with disbelief right after a big loss, before any anger.

facts.quote: Thereafter, moral indignation was experienced, followed by chasing behaviour, in an attempt to restore a 'fair balance' between wins and losses.
facts.claim: Then came a sense of unfairness, and players chased their losses to even the score.

facts.quote: It was also observed that experienced players, as compared to inexperienced ones, exhibited in their narratives a more mature disposition towards encountering 'bad luck', and losing in general.
facts.claim: Experienced players handled bad luck and losing more maturely than beginners.

facts.quote: You may have a Tilt problem and have no idea it’s Tilt
facts.claim: Tendler: you can have a tilt problem without knowing it's tilt.

facts.quote: After a 6% drawdown I immediately reduce to 10% max. After an 8% drawdown I reduce to 8% max. And after 10% drawdown I reduce to 5% max.
facts.claim: The owner's ladder: max position 10% after a 6% drawdown, 8% after 8%, 5% after 10%.

walkthroughs.title: What tilt is
steps: Tilt is a poker word. A loss or a bad break gets under your skin, and the emotion starts making your calls.
Jared Tendler coaches poker players and traders. His trading book names five kinds: hating to lose, mistakes, injustice, revenge and entitlement.
Revenge is behind many blowups. You size up and trade more to win it back, and the next loss can be bigger.

walkthroughs.title: Your circuit breaker
steps: Markets have circuit breakers. If the S&P 500 falls 7% in a day before 3:25 p.m., trading halts market-wide for 15 minutes.
Build your own: a daily loss limit, a cap on trades, and a break when the urge to break a rule hits.
Write them before the session, while you're calm. Once tilt builds, your mind can't stop it, so the rule has to.

walkthroughs.title: After a run of losses
steps: Losing streaks happen to the best traders. They can still mess with your head and your execution.
After a big loss, step away first. Come back smaller, and add size back only as your execution proves itself.
Here's our rule: after a 6% drawdown, max position size drops to 10%. Deeper drawdowns cut it further.

questions.q: What does it mean to be on tilt?
choices: You're letting emotion make calls
You're in a long losing streak
You've hit your daily loss limit
You're trading bigger than usual
questions.why: Emotion is making your trade calls. Researchers define tilt as out-of-control decisions driven by negative emotions. Tendler calls it a problem with anger in performance.
questions.lesson_line: Tilt isn't the loss. It's what the loss does to your next decision.

wrong.You're in a long losing streak: A streak can set tilt off, but streaks happen to good traders too. Tilt is the emotion taking over afterward.
wrong.You've hit your daily loss limit: That's the rule that stops tilt from costing more. It isn't tilt itself.
wrong.You're trading bigger than usual: That's a symptom tilt can cause. Tilt is the emotion behind it.

questions.q: Years of experience make a trader immune to tilt.
questions.why: False. In one study, experienced poker players took bad luck more maturely, but that isn't immunity. Pros at the Chicago Board of Trade still took extra risk to win back losing mornings.
questions.lesson_line: Nobody is immune to tilt. Written rules protect you when experience doesn't.

questions.q: You take a loss, then jump right back in with bigger size to make it back today. What's that called?
choices: Revenge trading
Averaging down a loser
Scaling in
Hedging
questions.why: Revenge trading. After losses, traders often try to make it back by raising the size and frequency of their trades. Tendler lists revenge as one of his kinds of tilt.
questions.lesson_line: The trade right after a loss gets the same rules as every other trade.

wrong.Averaging down a loser: That's adding to the same losing position. Revenge is a fresh trade, sized up, to win the loss back.
wrong.Scaling in: That's building a position in planned pieces. Nothing about it is a reaction to a loss.
wrong.Hedging: A hedge offsets risk you already hold. Revenge adds risk.

questions.q: You're down on the day. A long-shot trade that could get you back to even looks extra tempting. What's that pull called?
choices: The break-even effect
The house money effect
The disposition effect
questions.why: The break-even effect. Thaler and Johnson found that after losses, a chance to break even is especially attractive. Pros at the Chicago Board of Trade took extra afternoon risk to recover morning losses.
questions.lesson_line: Getting back to even is a feeling, not a setup.

wrong.The house money effect: That's the mirror image: taking more risk after a gain.
wrong.The disposition effect: That's holding losers too long and selling winners too soon. It isn't about chasing a way back to even.

questions.q: Fill in the first step of Tendler's real-time strategy.
questions.sentence: Step 1: ___ that your problem has been triggered.
questions.why: Recognize. You can't stop what you can't see, so his first step is noticing the trigger. Then you break the momentum, inject logic and use a reminder.
questions.lesson_line: Spot it early. The sooner you name it, the cheaper it is.

questions.q: If you don't feel angry, you can't be on tilt.
questions.why: False. Tendler says tilt can be a quiet seethe that leaves you distracted or bored, and you may not know it's tilt. In a study of poker players, tilt often began with plain disbelief after a big loss.
questions.lesson_line: Quiet tilt still costs money. Watch what you do, not only how you feel.

questions.q: Besides a daily loss limit, which rule best guards against rapid-fire revenge trades?
choices: A cap on trades per day
A tighter stop on every trade
A bigger watchlist to pick from
A daily profit target
questions.answer: A cap on trades per day
questions.why: A cap on trades per day. Tendler suggests firm controls on the number of trades a day, or a daily loss limit. Investopedia notes traders set rules on how many trades fit them.
questions.lesson_line: Count the clicks. A cap on trades stops a burst before it grows.

wrong.A tighter stop on every trade: That shrinks each loss but does nothing to stop the burst of trades.
wrong.A bigger watchlist to pick from: More names means more things to click. Overtrading often looks like buying anything that might be good.
wrong.A daily profit target: A target says when to stop on a good day. Revenge happens on the bad ones.

questions.q: You know your rule. Right after a big loss, you break it anyway. What's usually going on?
choices: Emotion is overriding your judgment
Your strategy stopped working
The rule doesn't fit this market
questions.why: Emotion is overriding your judgment. Tendler: when emotion runs too high, it limits your ability to make correct decisions. You can know it's wrong and still feel compelled to do it.
questions.lesson_line: You won't think your way out mid-tilt. Catch it early, or step away.

wrong.Your strategy stopped working: A strategy problem shows up in your log over many trades. Breaking a rule you know, right after a loss, is a decision problem.
wrong.The rule doesn't fit this market: That's the story the emotion tells you. If a rule needs changing, change it before the next session, not mid-loss.

questions.story: Two losses this morning. You trade liquid growth leaders. A $3 stock you've never traded is up 30%, and one good pop would get you even.
questions.q: What's really going on?
choices: A revenge pick outside your lane
Smart rotation into strength
A normal momentum entry today
Spotting a hot stock early on
questions.answer: A revenge pick outside your lane
questions.why: A revenge pick. It's outside what you know, picked for a quick win after losses. CIBC warns this can easily backfire, and the second loss can be bigger than the first.
questions.lesson_line: If it wasn't on your list before the open, it isn't a trade after two losses.

wrong.Smart rotation into strength: Rotation is a planned shift. This is a stock you'd never touch, picked because you're down.
wrong.A normal momentum entry today: A momentum entry comes from your setup and your list. The only reason here is getting even.
wrong.Spotting a hot stock early on: It may well be hot, but you've never traded it, and the reason you're looking is the loss.

questions.q: Your daily loss limit is 1.5% of a $40,000 account. You're down $410 so far. How much more can you lose before you stop?
questions.why: $190. Your limit is 1.5% of $40,000, and you've already used $410 of it. A trade that risks more than what's left could carry you past your line.
questions.lesson_line: Know your room before every trade. When it's gone, you're done for the day.

questions.q: Which of these works as a personal circuit breaker?
choices: Done for the day at a set loss
A stop-loss on every trade
Trade until you're back to even
questions.answer: Done for the day at a set loss
questions.why: Done for the day at a set loss. Schwab describes circuit breakers that block more trading after a set loss in a day. A stop guards one trade. The breaker guards the day.
questions.lesson_line: A stop protects the trade. A loss limit protects the account from you.

wrong.A stop-loss on every trade: Stops matter, but each one covers a single trade. Five stops in a row can still sink the day. Pros use both.
wrong.Trade until you're back to even: That's the break-even pull. It keeps you trading exactly when you think least clearly.

questions.story: Three trades today, three stops. Each one followed your plan.
questions.q: Does that mean you're on tilt?
choices: Not alone; watch your next move
Yes, three losses in a row is tilt
No, only a big loss causes tilt
Yes, so stop trading for the week
questions.answer: Not alone; watch your next move
questions.why: Not by itself. Losing streaks happen to the best of us. Tilt is the reaction: Tendler says the damage comes more from how you react to losing than from the loss.
questions.lesson_line: Losses aren't tilt. What you do after them can be.

wrong.Yes, three losses in a row is tilt: Losses are results. Tilt is emotion taking over your decisions after them.
wrong.No, only a big loss causes tilt: Small hits can stack up. Tendler says a run of triggers in a short time can tip you over.
wrong.Yes, so stop trading for the week: That treats a normal streak as a crisis. Watch your next decisions and let your preset limits decide.

questions.q: Tilt from one bad day can carry over into the next day's trades.
questions.why: True. Tendler says tilt can carry over day to day, making it easier to tilt again. Schwab notes the lingering effects of a big loss can slow your thinking.
questions.lesson_line: Tilt doesn't reset at the bell. Check yourself before the open, not only your charts.

questions.story: You get stopped out at 10 a.m. By 10:40 you've made six more trades. None of them were on your watchlist.
questions.q: What's going on?
choices: Overtrading to win it all back
Scalping, a valid fast style
Normal action on a busy day
Testing new setups live today
questions.answer: Overtrading to win it all back
questions.why: Overtrading to win back the loss. Traders often overtrade after a loss, raising size and frequency to recoup it. A burst of positions with no plan behind any of them is a telltale sign.
questions.lesson_line: Count your trades after a loss. A sudden burst is the tell.

wrong.Scalping, a valid fast style: Scalping is planned in advance. Six unplanned trades right after a stop-out is a reaction.
wrong.Normal action on a busy day: A busy market doesn't put stocks on your list. These trades came from the loss.
wrong.Testing new setups live today: A real test is planned, small and on purpose. This burst came straight out of a loss.

questions.q: You risk 1% a trade and lose three in a row. You double your risk to win it back, and that one stops out too. What's the day's total loss?
questions.why: 5%. Three 1% losses, then a doubled trade that loses twice as much. One revenge trade did the damage of two normal ones.
questions.lesson_line: Doubling up after losses doesn't dig you out faster. It digs the hole faster.

questions.story: Your account is 9% below its peak. A great setup shows up, and you want a full-size position to make some of it back.
questions.q: Under our drawdown rule, what's your max position size?
choices: 8% of the account
10% of the account
5% of the account
Full size, it's a great setup
questions.why: 8% of the account. Our rule: after a 6% drawdown, max size drops to 10%. After 8%, it's 8%. After 10%, it's 5%. At 9% down, the cap is 8%.
questions.lesson_line: The deeper the drawdown, the smaller the cap. A great setup doesn't change that.

wrong.10% of the account: That's the cap after a 6% drawdown. You're past 8%, so it's lower.
wrong.5% of the account: That kicks in at a 10% drawdown. You're at 9%.
wrong.Full size, it's a great setup: A great setup doesn't erase the drawdown. Sizing up to make it back is the revenge pull.

questions.story: A 2005 study followed pro traders at the Chicago Board of Trade. Some of them had a losing morning.
questions.q: What did the study find about their afternoon trading?
choices: Above-average risk to win it back
Lower risk to protect what's left
No change from their usual trading
Most stopped trading for the day
questions.answer: Above-average risk to win it back
questions.why: Above-average risk to win it back. Coval and Shumway found these pros regularly took extra afternoon risk to recover morning losses. Pros feel the pull too.
questions.lesson_line: Even pros chase a losing morning. That's why the rule goes in writing.

wrong.Lower risk to protect what's left: That's what large institutions did in their currency trades, in a different study. These Chicago traders did the opposite.
wrong.No change from their usual trading: The study found a clear shift after a losing morning: more risk, not the same.
wrong.Most stopped trading for the day: That's the circuit breaker habit, and it's the right one. It isn't what this study found.

questions.q: In a Chicago Board of Trade study, pros down on the morning paid up to buy and sold for less.
questions.why: True. In the Chicago Board of Trade study, losing traders bought above and sold below the prices that came just before. Those prices reversed faster than other traders' prices.
questions.lesson_line: When you need a trade, you pay for it.

questions.story: You followed your plan, but a surprise downgrade gapped your stock through the stop. You're well inside your daily loss limit. You want to buy something, now.
questions.q: Your loss limit hasn't tripped. What now?
choices: Pause anyway; the urge warns you
Keep going, since the limit decides
Buy it back now to get even
Double size on the next good setup
questions.answer: Pause anyway; the urge warns you
questions.why: Pause anyway. Schwab's example rule: take 15 minutes when you feel an urge to break a trading rule. In a study of poker players, that 'not fair' feeling after a loss was followed by chasing.
questions.lesson_line: Under the limit doesn't mean in control. The urge is your cue to pause.

wrong.Keep going, since the limit decides: The limit stops a bad day from getting worse. The urge is the earlier warning, and Tendler says to catch emotion early.
wrong.Buy it back now to get even: That's buying to get even, not buying a setup.
wrong.Double size on the next good setup: That's revenge sizing. If it fails, the loss is twice the size.

questions.q: Once tilt starts, you'll notice it in time to stop yourself.
questions.why: False. Tendler: once emotion gets too intense, the mind can't stop it, and spotting it afterward is like seeing a trade you missed. Set the limits while you're calm.
questions.lesson_line: Don't count on catching it late. Set the rule early.

questions.story: Your rule: done for the day at a 1.5% loss. Today so far: -0.5%, -0.5%, +0.2%, -0.7%. At 2 p.m. a textbook setup appears.
questions.q: What does your rule say?
choices: Stop: you're down 1.5%, the limit
Take it, a great setup is different
Take it at half size
Take it, one winner gets you even
questions.why: Stop. You're down 1.5% on the day, and that's your line. Once you reach your limit, Investopedia says, trading on is unsound.
questions.lesson_line: The limit doesn't care how good the next one looks. That's the point of it.

wrong.Take it, a great setup is different: Every setup looks great when you want the day back. The rule exists for exactly this moment.
wrong.Take it at half size: Half size still breaks a rule you set when you were calm.
wrong.Take it, one winner gets you even: That's the break-even pull: a chance to get back to even looks extra good after losses.

questions.story: A tilt day cost you 4% last week. Since then you've cut your size and taken eight trades, all by your plan.
questions.q: When does your size go back to normal?
choices: While your execution holds up
Right away, to win back the 4%
After your next big winner
Never, staying small is safer
questions.why: As your execution keeps holding up. Schwab: raise size as you show a new track record of running your system. Tendler: once you size up without hurting execution, settle in before the next step.
questions.lesson_line: Earn your size back with execution, one step at a time.

wrong.Right away, to win back the 4%: That's revenge on a delay. The 4% comes back through good trades, not bigger ones.
wrong.After your next big winner: One winner is one result. P&L isn't a reliable measure over the short term.
wrong.Never, staying small is safer: Too far. Size is meant to come back once your results and execution are back on track.

conflicts: Tendler's tilt types: his poker book named seven; his trading book keeps five (he took out Run Bad and Desperation, per s10). Only his own site names the types, so no question is keyed on a type's label: the five appear in walk-through w1 and, attributed to him, in the why of q03. (Checker, 2026-11-09: q19's 'Tendler calls it injustice tilt' was removed, because his page lists the label without defining it.) Keys rest on the behaviour (revenge, injustice leading to chasing), which other publishers back.

Tilt definition: Tendler (s10) calls tilt a problem with ANGER; the peer-reviewed definition (s19) says NEGATIVE EMOTIONS more broadly, and its stories begin with disbelief, then moral indignation. q01's key ('Emotion is making your trade calls') and q06 fit both readings.

Experience and tilt: s19 (2013) found experienced players took bad luck more maturely; the same group's 2014 Journal of Gambling Studies paper (link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10899-012-9339-4) found experience associated with MORE severe tilting in the long run. The 2014 paper and Moreau et al. 2020 (perceived vs measured tilt, link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10899-019-09903-7) were dropped because Springer serves a bot challenge to the quote checker's client (the text is in the page for curl, so the checker read MISSING). q02 keys only what both papers allow: experience does not make anyone immune. (Checker, 2026-11-09: the why said flatly 'Experience helps', which the 2014 paper does not support; summaries of it say experienced players may tilt less per hand but more in the long run. The why now reports only the 2013 finding, as one study, and says it is not immunity.)

api/data/voice_kb/trading_principles.json (bb-003, a draft recall item in docs/study/bank/recall.principles.json) says 'trades placed within 5 minutes of a loss have a 30% lower win rate' and prescribes 'the next trade must be 50% smaller, OR a 15-minute mandatory break'. No source was found for the 30% figure or the rule; nothing here uses it. This unit's 15-minute pause is Schwab's own example (f25), stated as an example.

Coval and Shumway (s16): summaries of the full paper put the extra afternoon risk at about 15 or 16 percent more likely (versions differ). The file uses only the abstract's qualitative finding, never a number.

Schwab, 'How to Recover From a Big Trading Loss' (schwab.com/learn/story/how-to-recover-from-big-trading-loss, Joe Mazzola, 2026-03-09) illustrates a trader who 'never risks more than 5% of their trading portfolio on a single trade': far above the 2% ceiling in sizing_rule.md section 1 (a line not marked as the owner's answer, so the track asks it as a house rule nowhere; see F8.05 and F9.02 conflicts), and it also discusses taxes. Read, not cited.
Schwab s8 ties revenge trading to cortisol and stress hormones. Only its sentence linking revenge trading to blowups (f19) is cited; the physiology is not taught.

The SEC hot-stock alert (s3) also lists 'momentum investing' among risky behaviours. Only its lines on emotional, impulsive decisions and pressure to act are cited. The SEC Director's Take (s2) says it is no longer updated; it is cited only for the timeless line on emotions and costly mistakes.

FINRA: the units plan names 'FINRA on overtrading'. FINRA's excessive-trading material is about brokers churning client accounts; Investopedia (s5) confirms those rules cover brokers, not a trader's own account. No FINRA page on self-directed overtrading or tilt was found, so FINRA is not cited.

Drawdown ladder (h01): the owner's own published words (2026-07-19), quoted in docs/study/sizing_rule.md section 4, where section 8 still asks him to confirm them as the house protocol (the curriculum dossier's '-5% halve, -10% pilot only' is not a source and is not used). q16 asks it as 'our drawdown rule' once, at a 9% drawdown, to stay clear of F9.04's planned '-7%' case.

The units row mentions the Journal's tilt rules (rapid fire, loss streak, daily loss approach, cooling off). Those live in app code, not in a house source the contract allows, so they are not quoted as our rules; the unit teaches the same ideas (trade cap, loss limit, pause) from Schwab, Investopedia and Tendler.
